### CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR
</header>

3222. Furthermore, loves and their affections are represented by flames, and this with an inexpressible variety. Truths, however, are represented by lights, and by innumerable modifications of light. From this it can be established why it is that in the Word, the goods which belong to love are signified by flames, and the truths which belong to faith are signified by lights.

3223. There are two <term>Luces</term> <gloss>Lights</gloss> by which man is illuminated: the Light of the world and the Light of heaven. The Light of the world is from the sun; the Light of heaven is from the Lord. The Light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for those things which are in him. Although the things there do not appear to belong to that light, they nevertheless do; for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus unless they have some form from the light and shade there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which matter so much in the natural man that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. But the Light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and ascribes "light" to it. The reason is that as long as he is in worldly and corporeal things, he only has a perception of such things as belong to the light of the world, but not of such things as belong to the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the entire heaven is in 그 light. This Light of heaven is indeed immensely more perfect than the light of the world. Those things which make up a single ray in the light of the world make up myriads in the Light of heaven. Intelligence and wisdom are within the light of heaven. It is that light which flows into the light of the world that is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive the objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, man would never have any perception, for the things which belong to the light of the world have their life from there. Between those Lights—or between those things which are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world—a <term>correspondentia</term> <gloss>correspondence</gloss> exists when the external or natural man acts as one with the internal or spiritual man, that is, when the former serves the latter; and the things which then exist in the light of the world are <term>repræsentativa</term> <gloss>representatives</gloss> of such things as are in the light of heaven.

3224. It is strange that man does not yet know that his intellectual mind is in a certain light which is altogether different from the light of the world; but such is the condition that to those who are in the Light of the world, the Light of heaven is like darkness, and to those who are in the Light of heaven, the light of the world is like darkness. This comes principally from loves, which are the heats of light. Those who are in the loves of self and of the world—and thus only in the heat of the light of the world—are affected only by evils and falsities, and these are the things which extinguish the truths which belong to the light of heaven. <summary>Swedenborg explains that spiritual truths and loves are represented as light and flame respectively. He distinguishes between the light of the world, which governs the natural man's sense of time and space, and the light of heaven, which provides intelligence and flows into the natural mind to enable perception.</summary>
